name: Livoletide
lead: Livoletide (AZP-531) is a cyclic peptide analogue of unacylated ghrelin that was developed to treat hyperphagia, the intense and persistent hunger, in Prader-Willi syndrome (PWS).[1][2] Its appearance-related interest stems from its status as an experimental appetite and body-weight drug.

Its pivotal phase 2b/3 trial, ZEPHYR, enrolled 158 participants and is recorded on ClinicalTrials.gov as terminated.[3][4] It has not been approved, and no study has tested it for cosmetic fat loss in people without PWS.

paras: PWS is a rare genetic disorder in which infancy is marked by feeding difficulty and a later stage brings hyperphagia and obesity. At the time the livoletide programme was described there was no approved treatment for the hyperphagia.[1][5]

People with PWS have been reported to have a relative deficit of unacylated ghrelin compared with acylated ghrelin, which led to the hypothesis that replacing it would reduce hyperphagia.[2][5] Livoletide is a cyclic peptide analogue of unacylated ghrelin. Nonclinical and juvenile toxicity studies were presented at endocrine meetings.[2][6]

A conference abstract reported that livoletide improved hyperphagia and food-related behaviours in both obese and non-obese people with PWS in an earlier study.[5] The ZEPHYR phase 2b/3 randomised, placebo-controlled trial (NCT03790865), started in March 2019 with 158 participants, is listed as terminated.[3][4]
A preprint reported that unacylated ghrelin and AZP-531 suppressed the growth of breast cancer cells in three-dimensional cultures; this is laboratory work only.[7]

timeline.event: ZEPHYR phase 2b/3 trial begins in Prader-Willi syndrome.[3][4]

card.summary: An investigational unacylated-ghrelin peptide built for Prader-Willi hunger, with its pivotal trial terminated.
card.note: Never approved; no studies in people seeking cosmetic fat loss.

quick.overview:
Livoletide is an experimental peptide designed to curb the extreme hunger of Prader-Willi syndrome. It mimics unacylated ghrelin, a form of the hunger hormone that does not activate the usual ghrelin receptor.

Its main phase 2b/3 trial was terminated, and no study has tested it for appearance-related fat loss.
quick.mechanism: It replaces a reported relative deficit of unacylated ghrelin in people with PWS, with the hypothesis that this reduces hyperphagia.
quick.risks: It is investigational and unapproved. Safety information in the sources is limited to nonclinical and juvenile toxicity work and trial records.
